rules: Prior context is for disambiguation only.
Do not use prior context as evidence for new L1 candidates.
Every new L1 candidate must cite only the current transcript or current idea units.

items.content: An experiment is planned to compare the proposed 'dynamic' chunking method against 'fixed-size' chunking baselines (e.g., 3-turn or 1-turn chunks). The evaluation will measure both efficiency, by counting the number of LLM requests, and quality, using precision and recall against a ground truth.
Devise a method to prove the value of the proposed memory architecture compared to a system without it.

An ablation study is planned to validate the memory architecture. It will compare four conditions: a RAG-only baseline, a short-term memory only system, a long-term memory only system, and the full combined system. Working memory will be active in all conditions.

An experiment is planned to compare a dynamic, content-aware chunking strategy against a fixed-size chunking baseline. To ensure a fair comparison, the fixed-size chunk will be set to the average length of the chunks produced by the dynamic method. The evaluation will measure both computational cost (e.g., number of computations) and performance, using precision and recall against a human-annotated ground truth. A successful outcome is considered a direct and significant project result.

The retrieval strategy for the hierarchical memory involves first matching a query against detailed L1 nodes, and then including the corresponding L2 and L3 ancestor nodes in the results. This provides both specific details and high-level context.

The evaluation strategy will be structured around three categories of questions: 1) short-term correctness of recent answers, 2) long-term evolution of a topic over time, and 3) the reasoning behind current decisions. The primary metric will be correctness and completeness, assessed by comparing the agent's output against a ground-truth answer.

Evaluation questions will be divided into three categories: 1) Short-term: verifying the correctness of recent answers. 2) Long-term evolution: asking for the complete progression of a topic over time. 3) Decision reasoning: asking for the rationale behind current decisions based on past discussions.

An experiment to compare the trade-offs of different long-term memory processing methods (incremental chunking, fixed-size chunking, and iterative sentence merging) was deferred. The team is proceeding with the incremental method on the assumption that it is effective, particularly at filtering out irrelevant chatter, but this has not been experimentally validated.

The system will process transcripts using a dynamic chunking mechanism instead of fixed-size chunks. An LLM, via Function Calling (e.g., a `Read(start_line, end_line)` function), will autonomously and iteratively determine the number of lines to read. The LLM's decision is based on achieving semantic completeness, ensuring that a full thought or dialogue exchange is captured within a chunk before processing.

A forgetting mechanism will be implemented for Long-Term Memory (LTM) where a node's relevancy score decays over time if not referenced. "Forgotten" nodes are not deleted but are deprioritized, and can be revived if the topic is mentioned again, causing their score to increase.

To handle topics that fade and reappear, a memory node's 'recency' score decays over time, but its 'importance' score establishes a floor, preventing the recency from decaying to zero. This ensures that important but dormant topics remain retrievable.

The team is debating whether to adopt a multi-agent architecture or continue with the current monolithic, tool-calling system. A proposed plan is to first try modifying the existing prompts to make the agent's behavior more explicit, and only then decide on the architecture.
